description: Learn how to exploit a heap overflow with Data Execution Prevention and Address Space Layout Randomization enabled, in order to get a shell.
goal:
Your goal is to exploit the executable which is listening on port 5000 of the vulnbox, in order to get a shell.

You have to do it with ASLR enabled (it is enabled by default).

Some files will be provided to you for the analysis:

  • Original executable file: heappy
  • Libc used by the executable inside Docker image: libc-2.19.so
  • Ld interpreter used by the executable inside Docker image: ld-2.19.so
  • Patched executable file, which will look for libc-2.19.so and ld-2.19.so in its current directory: heappy_patchelf

For your convenience, if you don't want to do reverse engineering of the executable, we also provide the source code.

We recommend to create a script to automate the interaction, especially to send not-printable bytes.

If you do, on your host system:

docker pull shotokhan/attacker_heap_overflow_nx

You get an attacker box that you can start as an hack tool, with all the challenge files and all the tools you need!

A hint for you if your exploit works locally and not remotely: you interact with the program over a TTY, therefore some characters are stripped; to overcome this filter, you have to prepend special characters (like null bytes) with \x16.
solution:
For the exploit we used the following tools:

  • gdb
  • ltrace
  • pwntools
  • one_gadget

 At first, we do some static analysis of the executable.

We can see that it is a 64-bit executable, with little endian format, and that is is dynamically linked.

We also use an utility provided by pwntools, called checksec, to check the security protections of the executable.

There aren't canary values to protect the stack frame, but stack is not executable (heap will also be not executable).

Now, let's interact with the program to see how it behaves under normal conditions.

It's time to look for bugs. We'll give a look at the source code first, then we'll make some dynamic analysis using gdb.

 

On line 79 we can see that function choose_language is called:

choose_language(&f);

On line 53 we can find its code. This function, each time it's called, allocates a new chunk to store a functions struct:

struct functions {
  void (*greeting)(char* name);
  void (*menu)();
  void (*choose_name)();
};

From the overall code, we can observe 2 things:

  1. choose_language can be called multiple times within the interaction, and this allows us to allocate new chunks to our pleasure.
  2. functions struct contains pointers to functions, to distinguish between Italian and English language.

On line 80 we can observe how it is allocated a chunk for data struct, which will contain the user's name.

struct data {
  char name[128];
};

On lines 82 and 91 we can notice that the function which allows the user to insert a name introduces a vulnerability in the program.

scanf("%s", d->name);

Indeed, it doesn't check input size and writes the just inserted name into heap.

It is the case of heap overflow.

Let's debug the program.

We stop the execution of the program before inserting the name, and look at main function's disassembly.

By comparing source code and disassembly, we decide to put a breakpoint on the first function call in the while loop, related to the call of greeting (ita_greeting or en_greeting) function, which is also the first in the functions struct. We do this to view the state of the process before it prints out the greeting.

(gdb) break *0x400921

Let's continue the execution of the program by inserting AAAAAAAA as name.

The breakpoint gets activated and we can look at registers' values.

In rdi register there is the first (and only) parameter passed to the function, that is the pointer to data chunk (and so it's the pointer to "name", the first and only element of the struct); therefore, rdi contains an heap address, and if we inspect that memory in gdb we can find the previously inserted name: AAAAAAAA (0x41 is A in hex format).

(gdb) x/200xb 0x1a45030

We can notice that there isn't any return address to overwrite, like we're used to do when performing stack overflow; in fact, it is an heap overflow, and performing the overflow now would not lead to a behaviour useful for an attacker.

We recall that, after the choice of a name, it's possible to change language and, as previously said, choose_language function allocates a new chunk in the heap, this time next to data chunk, and with function pointers inside.

This particular is also well depicted by ltrace:

Now we can perform the overflow and overwrite a function pointer.

Let's keep debugging to verify what we said.

We'll inspect the heap again, as we did before.

Starting from 0x1a450c0, in the following 8 bytes we see a memory address (in little endian format: we know this is the format because of the output of file command, executed at the start), and, if what we said previously was correct, this should be the address of ita_greeting function (because, if you look at the interaction, we chose Italian language), that is 0x4006bd.

We were right. Now, ideally, we would replace this function pointer with the address of an executable memory area in which we have put a shellcode.

To summarize, we execute the program, choosing the language, choosing a name, then changing the language to make sure that we have a chunk allocated next to the chunk we're able to overflow, and then changing the name to perform the actual overflow to overwrite the function pointer.

The problem is that we can't insert a shellcode in the buffer allocated for the name and jump to it, because that buffer is within the heap, which is not executable.

So we need to find another way to open a shell.

We can look inside libc to find some functions to jump at; then, replace the functions pointer with the address of some libc function which open a shell.

The next problem to overcome is getting libc's base address, because there is ASLR enabled.

Let's use, then, an attack called Format String attack, to get libc's base address. printf function takes as first parameter a string, which it interprets as a "format string": inside this string there can be control sequences (denoted as format specifiers), like "%d", "%s" and so on, which tell printf function to take parameters of some specified type from the stack and print them inside the format string, replacing the format specifiers. When you call printf in C, usually you explicitly pass parameters to it; what happens if printf is called without parameters but still have format specifiers? It happens that it takes as parameter everything that is located on the stack, and it's possible to have an arbitrary number of parameters. Furthermore, by "playing" with format specifiers, it's also possible to have a direct access to parameters, instead of a positional access (for example, "%7$d" is "print as an integer the 7th parameter").

References to this type of attack: https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/Format_string_attack

So, now we want to overwrite the address of ita_greeting with the address of printf. We need printf address inside our program (we know that there is a printf address because many functions call printf!).

We can find it with pwntools, using as executable heappy_patchelf (for now we could also use heappy, but later we will need the patched one, so it's better if we start working with it now).

We can check that the address we found (0x400580) is actually the address of printf, in gdb.

This printf is not libc's printf, but is from PLT: printf@plt is a wrapper around libc's printf; the actual address of libc's printf can be found in the GOT, and is denoted as printf@got.

Let's continue with the execution of the program and, when it asks us for the name, we send a payload composed of padding until the function pointer to replace and the address 0x400580 in little endian format.

The amount of padding is 144 bytes, this can be seen by looking at the heap layout and comparing the addresses of the data chunk and of the functions chunk.

Therefore, we're able to overwrite the first function pointer with the address of printf@plt.

Actually, as long as the function which takes user input is a scanf, we need to consider one less byte in the payload: this is because it adds a null byte, which would overwrite the LSB of the next function pointer, which could result in strange behaviour or even in a segmentation fault; we don't have problems because the last byte of our payload is already a null byte.

The result we obtain in the heap, if we correctly send the payload, is the following:

Now we're able to perform the format string attack; recall that our target is to obtain a libc address, to compute the base address from it.

We need to spot what input we need to give to printf, in order to reach our target.

Let's look at the stack layout, then:

We try to give different inputs to printf in order to print a pointer to libc, for example "%10$p", "%11$p", until we find what we look for.

After some tries, we see that the 13th parameter on the stack ("%13$p") is a juicy fruit.

In fact, as we'll see shortly, it is the main function's return address.

Note: the stack layout represented below is not the same layout as seen by printf during the elaboration of format specifiers.

 We can see using info proc mappings (in gdb) that the highlighted address is mapped to the memory allocated to libc.

In particular, if we disassemble the bytes at the previously highlighted address:

disas 0x7f1f53160f45

This libc function is called __libc_start_main and is called at start of the program, before calling the main.

So, with the previously mentioned format string, we obtain the address of an instruction inside __libc_start_main function. Recall that our target is to obtain libc's base address.

Note: the address space is random but relative offsets are kept unchanged.

By subtracting the value 245 at main's return address, we obtain the address of __libc_start_main: 0x00007f1f53160e50.

The value is 245 because the following instruction is the return address of the main:

Now we need to obtain the offset of __libc_start_main w.r.t. libc base address.

As previously pointed, the offset is always constant, what changes at any execution is libc's base address.

We look for the offset in libc-2.19.so.

Therefore, to obtain libc's base address, we need to subtract this offset (0x0000000000021e50) to the address of __libc_start_main previously found.

After having obtained libc's base address, we need to look for a function to open a shell.

Actually, we don't need to jump at the start of a function: we can jump at any point in the program.

What we'll do is looking for one or more gadgets that allow us to open a shell.

A gadget is a sequence of variable-length instructions that belong to a code that already exists, for
example a sequence of bytes in the .text section of the program can be interpreted as a gadget, as long as
they are valid opcodes.
Gadgets are similar to functions, in fact they have to give control back to the main program when they end; for
this reason we are searching for gadgets which have ret, jmp or call as last instruction in assembly code.
For more informations follow the link below:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return-oriented_programming

Tipically, gadgets are used in buffer overflow attacks on the stack, but we are acting on the heap, so we have to use
JOP (Jump Oriented Programming) instead of ROP (Return Oriented Programming).

We are in JOP conditions because we're not using the stack pointer, which change positions automatically, acting as a dispatcher with the ret instruction; for this reason, we have to find indirect (or indirect with offset) jump operations to registers. If it isn't clear, see this answer:

https://security.stackexchange.com/a/201247

Now, the first thing to do is to find a gadget which helps us to open a shell by avoiding a long chain of gadgets; this kind of gadget is known as One-Gadget RCE.

To look for it, we use the tool one_gadget; it tipically discover gadgets which require one or more constraints to be satisfied.

We are searching for gadget in libc, so we can use the command:

one_gadget libc-2.19.so

The tool shows us the following output.

We notice that, at run time (looking at the process state when it is at any gadget's first instruction), we don’t respect any constraint, so we have to find an intermediate gadget which allow us to respect one of this constraints and let us jump to the correct one_gadget’s address.

Going back to look at the state of the program at the breakpoint we set, we can see that rdi and rdx registers contain name's buffer address, which is allocated in heap memory. For mantaining control, we have to find a gadget which terminates with an instruction of indirect jump to rdi or rdx register.

We can use another tool, named ROPgadget, that is shipped with pwntools, which discover gadgets having last instruction "ret", "jmp" or "call".

Documentation of the tool: https://github.com/JonathanSalwan/ROPgadget

Let's try to find an intermediate gadget for the first one_gadget. The first idea that comes to mind is putting 0 in rax with an instruction "xor rax, rax", so we'll query all the gadgets with this instruction (we'll use grep instead of ROPgadget's options) which terminates with an indirect jump to rdi or rdx:

ROPgadget --binary libc-2.19.so | grep "xor rax, rax" | grep "jmp qword ptr [[]rd"

This query doesn't give us any result; we try with some other ideas, but couldn't find any way to respect the constraint while giving control back to the one_gadget.

So we went on with the second one_gadget.

Where rsp is the stack pointer, so we have to set at zero the value in [rsp + 0x30].

If you look at the stack layout when you're at the breakpoint we set before, it seems like the constraint is respected:

But, actually, the next instruction is callq *%rax, that will push the return address on the stack, so the constraint will not be respected at the state related to the gadget's first instruction. To respect the constraint, we have to perform a pop on the stack, then as usual we have to jmp to the other gadget.

So we search for the intermediate gadget with this command:

ROPgadget --binary libc-2.19.so | grep "pop" | grep "jmp qword ptr [[]rd"

In the following output, we choose as intermediate gadget the highlighted one.

Gadget:

0x0000000000198aec : pop rax ; xor al, 0xed ; jmp qword ptr [rdx]

Thanks to pop instruction, we can set zero the value [rsp + 0x30]; the xor operation is not harmful to us, and the jump instruction sets the instruction pointer to the first 8 bytes (qword) in the buffer obtained by de-referencing rdx (remember that rdi register memorizes the address of name chunk, because the name is the first parameter of greeting function; rdx register is set at the same value because, if you look at the assembly instructions right before the callq *%rax, rdx is used as intermediate register to copy the chunk's address from the stack to rdi, by indirect access with offset to rbp).

Now, to get a shell, we have to request another change name, and perform another heap overflow, setting the first 8 bytes of the name to the address of the one_gadget we chose, and setting the next chunk's function pointer to the address of the intermediate gadget.

Let's automate the attack.

We created a Python script called exploit.py to execute the attack automatically; it works both locally and remotely.

P.S.: the remote terminal modifies or strips some special characters because it's pseudo-TTY, so we have to prepend each special character with \x16 to make sure to give an intact payload to the process.

Let's have a look at the script:

We can describe what the script does in the following points:

  • From line 14 to 17, we are preparing the first payload, that makes an heap overflow overwriting the pointer to greeting with the address of the printf@plt function;
  • From line 18 to 27, we obtain the heap layout which allows us to control the instruction pointer with an overflow;
  • On line 29, we send the payload;
  • From line 33 to 35, we perform a format string attack obtaining the 13th parameter on the stack which contains the return address of main function;
  • From line 36 to 38, we compute the base address of libc;
  • On lines 46 and 47, we obtain the addresses of the two gadgets;
  • From line 48 to 52, we are going to wrap (escape) the characters of the gadgets if we are not working with a local process;
  • From line 53 to 58, we compose the second payload, then we send it, making sure that there aren't any of the 3 characters that would compromise the behaviour of the scanf (otherwise, just re-run the exploit);
  • From line 59 to 62, we flush some of the input we received before getting the shell, we disable some terminal features if we're working remotely to make sure we can get the output of the shell after the execve (which may cause some troubles with TTY), and then we switch to interactive mode, to have an interactive shell.

We hope you enjoyed!
